1. Foundations: science, theory and the scientific method

TermDefinition
ScienceTestable statements (hypothesis, law, model, theory) that explain natural phenomena through repeated observation and experiment.
ExperimentA controlled procedure that tests a phenomenon and finds cause and effect between variables (e.g. fixed temperature and pressure).
TheoryA testable framework of postulates that explains a phenomenon as cause and effect between variables.
LawA statement based on a large number of experimental observations (e.g. Ohm’s law).

What a good theory does

  • Explains phenomena, why they occur, and cause and effect between variables.
  • Explains the meaning of experimental data.
  • Predicts something new and guides experimentalists.
  • Has broad scope: covers a larger set of data.
KEY IDEANo direct experimental evidence? Test indirectly with thought experiments (mathematical and philosophical reasoning).

2. Logical reasoning and the scientific method

  • Logical reasoning is the process of using facts, evidence and clear thinking to reach a correct conclusion.
  • A rational argument has premises (base statements, evidence, observations) and a conclusion (a judgement derived from them).
LECTURE EXAMPLEPremise 1: metal A expands on heating.
Premise 2: metal B expands on heating.
Conclusion: all metals expand on heating.
The premises are specific observations and the conclusion is a general law.

The scientific method

A systematic investigation of a natural phenomenon, with the Ohm’s law example:

3. Types of variables

VariableMeaningExample (Ohm’s)
IndependentThe variable we change on our own; it does not depend on the other variable in that experimentVoltage V
DependentDepends on the other variables and changes when the independent variable changesCurrent I
ConstantA quantity that stays the same in the experiment
ControlledA variable held fixed externallyTemperature, resistance or length of the conductor

Graph of independent against dependent variable

  • Independent variable on the horizontal (x) axis, dependent on the vertical (y) axis. In Ohm’s experiment: V along x, I along y.
  • Sample data: V = 1, I = 1, R = 1 and V = 2, I = 2, R = 1. R is constant, so the plot is a straight line through the origin.
  • Slope = tan θ = ΔI / ΔV = 1/R, which gives ΔV = ΔI · R.

4. Physical quantities

  • A physical quantity can be measured accurately with an instrument, e.g. length with a meter scale or mass with a balance. Quantities such as happiness cannot be measured with a device and are called un-physical quantities.
  • They are measurable, describe the properties of an object, and are used in laws, theories and models. We test a hypothesis, law, model or theory by measuring physical quantities.

The seven SI base quantities

QuantityUnitSymbol
Lengthmetrem
Masskilogramkg
Timeseconds
Electric currentampereA
TemperaturekelvinK
Amount of substancemolemol
Luminous intensitycandelacd

Derived: volume (4/3 πr³ for a sphere, L³ for a cube). Velocity v = dl/dt → LT−1; acceleration a = d²l/dt² → LT−2; charge Q = It (dQ = I dt, integrate) → A·s.

Extra: why is current a scalar even though it has a direction?

Current flows along the wire, but it does not obey the vector (triangle) law. At a junction the total is the plain sum I = I₁ + I₂, not the vector sum of two arrows at an angle. A quantity that does not add like a vector is not a vector.

1. Vectors and physical quantities

SIMPLE DEFINITIONA vector is a quantity with both magnitude and direction that adds by the vector (triangle) law. A scalar has magnitude only.

What “tensor of rank one” means

Rank is the number of indices needed to label a quantity’s components. So a vector is a tensor of rank one.

Vector space properties

A vector space is a set where adding elements and multiplying them by numbers always gives another element of the set. Laws:

  1. Closure: adding two elements, or multiplying one by a scalar, gives another element of the space.
  2. Associative law of addition and multiplication.
  3. Commutative law of addition and multiplication.
  4. Inverse element.
  5. Identity element.

2. Vector space and invariance proofs

Show by closure that a 2×2 matrix is a vector

Add two 2×2 matrices entry by entry and you get another 2×2 matrix (closed under addition). Multiplying by a scalar k multiplies every entry by k, giving another 2×2 matrix (closed under scalar multiplication).

The other vector-space laws also hold, so 2×2 matrices form a vector space and each matrix is a vector.

Show that a combination of eikx and e−ikx is a vector

ψ=Aeikx+Be−ikx
Addition: ψ₁ + ψ₂ = (A₁ + A₂)eikx + (B₁ + B₂)e−ikx.
Scalar multiplication: cψ = (cA)eikx + (cB)e−ikx.
Closure holds, so ψ is a vector.

Position vector is invariant under rotation of coordinates

In 2D, r = x i + y j, x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, |r| = √(x² + y²). Rotate the axes by φ:

x′=xcosφ+ysinφy′=ycosφ−xsinφ​

Square and add. The cross terms 2xy sin φ cos φ cancel and cos²φ + sin²φ = 1, so:

∣r′∣=x′2+y′2​=x2+y2​=∣r∣

The magnitude is unchanged, so the position vector is invariant.

3. Principles of relativity

GALILEAN RELATIVITYPrinciple: all laws of mechanics remain the same in all inertial frames of reference. An inertial frame is one that is at rest or moves with constant velocity (no acceleration).

Invariance of Newton’s law in inertial frames

Setup: frames S (x, y, z, t) at rest and S′ (x′, y′, z′, t′) moving with constant velocity v along the x-axis. They coincide at t = 0. After time t, S′ has moved vt. A ball of mass m at P has velocity u′ relative to S′ and u relative to S.

Quick check: two velocities in the same direction subtract (V = v₁ − v₂), in opposite directions they add (V = v₁ + v₂).

Principles of special relativity

  • Postulate 1: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
  • Postulate 2: the speed of light in vacuum, c, is the same for all inertial observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
  • Galilean addition fails near the speed of light. The correct transformations are the Lorentz transformations, which mix space and time, giving time dilation and length contraction.
  • Galilean relativity is the low-speed limit (v ≪ c) of special relativity.
  • Maxwell’s equations are not invariant under Galilean transformations, but are under Lorentz transformations: a main motivation for special relativity.
x′=γ(x−vt)t′=γ(t−c2vx​)γ=1−v2/c2​1​​

ExampleBohr’s atomic theory, energy band theoryLasers, semiconductors, sensors, detectors

Basic criteria of a physical theory

It must be testable, explain natural phenomena and the meaning of experimental data, explain cause and effect, predict something new, guide experimentalists, and have broad scope.

1. Electric charge and fundamental charges

  • Charge is an intrinsic property of any material object, due to which it interacts with other objects.
  • More fundamentally, charge is a quantum number, defined to explain the properties and interactions of matter observed in experiments.

Types of charge

2. Fundamental structure of nucleons

  • Nucleons are protons and neutrons. Each is made of three quarks.
  • Quarks have spin 1/2 and carry colour charge (red, green, blue). A nucleon is colourless overall, with one quark of each colour.
PAULI AND COLOURPauli exclusion principle: no two identical fermions (spin-1/2 particles such as quarks and electrons) can occupy the same quantum state. In a proton the two u quarks are identical, so they must differ in another quantum number, which is why quarks have colour.

3. Fields and their fundamental nature

  • A field is a region of space in which every point is represented by a physical quantity, scalar or vector.
  • Fields are fundamental in modern physics. Particles are quanta of their fields: the photon is a quantum of the electromagnetic field and the electron is a quantum of the electron field.

4. Types and sources of fields

Electrostatics is the branch of physics that deals with the study of electric charges at rest.

1. Coulomb’s law

COULOMB’S LAWThe force between two stationary point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It acts along the line joining them: repulsive for like charges, attractive for unlike.
F=r2kq1​q2​​k=4πε0​1​≈9×109 Nm2/C2​

Vector form: F = k q₁q₂ r̂ / r², where r̂ is the unit vector along the line joining the charges.

Worked example

q₁ = 2 μC and q₂ = 3 μC at r = 10 cm.

F = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)(3×10⁻⁶) / (0.1)² F = 5.4 N (repulsive, both positive)

Superposition of forces and fields

The force between two charges is unaffected by the presence of other charges. For a test charge +q and sources +q₁ … +qₙ:

  1. Calculate F₁ on +q due to q₁, ignoring all others.
  2. Repeat for F₂, F₃, …, Fₙ, one at a time.
  3. The total force is the vector sum.
F=F1​+F2​+⋯+Fn​=i∑​Fi​=kqi∑​ri2​qi​r^i​​

This is the principle of superposition.

Limitations of Coulomb’s law

  1. Applies only to stationary charges
  2. Applies only to electric charges
  3. Applies only to point charges
  4. It diverges: as r → 0, F → ∞
  5. It violates the principle of causality (no information faster than light). It is silent about the mechanism by which force is transferred; this is also the principle of locality.

2. Electric field and electric field intensity

To make Coulomb’s law consistent with causality, Michael Faraday introduced the electric field. The force on a test charge +q due to a source Q happens in two steps:

Einstein introduced the gravitational field to overcome the same problem (Eg = F / m). Newton’s law of gravitation, F = G m₁m₂ / r², faced similar problems of non-locality.

Electric field intensity is the force per unit positive test charge:

E=qF​⟺F=qE
  • Field due to a point charge Q at distance r: E = kQ / r².
  • Many source charges: divide the superposed force by q. E = Σ k qᵢ r̂ᵢ / rᵢ²

Worked example

Q = 4 nC at r = 0.5 m.

E = (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁹) / (0.5)² E = 144 N/C

3. Continuous distribution of electric charge

Coulomb’s law can also be used for a continuous distribution of charge. For a line distribution on a wire, find the force on a test charge +q at point P at distance r from a small element dl.

  1. Line charge density λ = dq / dl, so dq = λ dl.
  2. Force on +q from the element dl, by Coulomb’s law:
  3. Total force from the whole line: integrate over the length.
dF=kqr2dq​r^=kqλr2dl​r^
F=kq∫r2λ​r^dl
DistributionDensityElement of charge
Linear (along a line)λ = dq / dldq = λ dl
Surface (over an area)σ = dq / dAdq = σ dA
Volume (throughout a volume)ρ = dq / dVdq = ρ dV

The same method works for all three, replacing dl by dA or dV. For the field, divide by q:

E=k∫r2dq​r^
BOARD QUESTIONDetermine the force on a charge +q placed at a distance from (i) a line distribution, (ii) a surface (areal) distribution and (iii) a volume distribution.

4. Electric flux

  • Electric flux measures how much electric field passes through an area. With field lines, it is proportional to the number of lines crossing the surface.
  • For a uniform field E through a flat area A, with θ the angle between E and the normal to the area:
ΦE​=EAcosθΦE​=∫E⋅dA​
  • Flux is maximum when the field is perpendicular to the surface (θ = 0), and zero when the field runs parallel to it (θ = 90°).
  • Unit: N m²/C. It is a scalar.

5. Electric dipole

  • An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and −q separated by a small distance d.
  • At r ≫ d: on the axis, E = 2kp / r³, along p. On the perpendicular bisector (equatorial line), E = kp / r³, opposite to p.
  • The dipole field falls as 1/r³, faster than the 1/r² of a single point charge, because the two fields partly cancel.

Lab Activity 2: errors and least count

  • Absolute error: Δx = |x measured − x true|, same unit as the quantity.
  • Zero error: reading when it should read zero. Positive if above zero, negative if below. True = observed − zero error.
  • Fractional uncertainty = Δx / x. Percentage = (Δx / x) × 100 %. Example: 20.0 ± 0.1 cm gives 0.005, or 0.5 %.
  • Least count (LC): smallest value an instrument can measure accurately. Plain scale: smallest division. Vernier: 1 MSD ÷ number of vernier divisions. Micrometer: pitch ÷ circular divisions.
InstrumentLeast count
Thermometer1 °C
Vernier callipers0.01 cm (0.1 mm)
Meter ruler0.1 cm (1 mm)
Stop watch0.01 s (digital)
Ammeter0.02 A (0–1 A, 50 divisions)
Voltmeter0.1 V (0–10 V, 100 divisions)
Galvanometer1 scale division
Top pan balance0.01 g
Protractor1°
Screw gauge0.01 mm

Positive ZE+ n × LC+ n × LC (n below 25)
Negative ZE− (10 − n) × LC− (50 − n) × LC (n above 25)

Self-test

Try the questions first. No peeking!

1. Why is current a scalar?Currents add as plain numbers at a junction (I = I₁ + I₂), not by the vector triangle law, so current is a scalar even though it has a direction along the wire.
2. Show that F = F′ under a Galilean transformation, in four steps.x = vt + x′, then u = v + u′, then a = a′ (v constant), then F = ma = ma′ = F′.
3. Charge of a proton and a neutron in terms of quark charges?Proton uud = 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1. Neutron udd = 2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0.
4. Force between 2 μC and 3 μC charges 10 cm apart?5.4 N (repulsive, since both charges are positive).
5. Electric field 0.5 m from a 4 nC point charge?144 N/C.
6. Name the five limitations of Coulomb’s law.Stationary charges only; electric charges only; point charges only; diverges as r → 0; violates causality / locality.
7. Vernier LC = 0.01 cm: MSR = 2.3 cm, VC = 6, ZE = +0.02 cm. True reading?Observed = 2.3 + 6 × 0.01 = 2.36 cm. True = 2.36 − 0.02 = 2.34 cm.
8. Name the three quantum revolutions and one application of each.First: atomic (energy level) theory, e.g. lasers. Second: energy band theory, e.g. transistors and chips. Third: quantum computing.
